headlines.article_text: Stock market today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu A trader works at the New York Stock Exchange on July 10, 2026. NYSE Stock futures rebounded on Sunday night as traders cautiously dipped a toe back in following last week's rout in shares linked to the artificial intelligence trend. Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked 0.2% higher, or 110 points. S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%. Stable oil prices early Sunday also lent the equity market some support. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 1.65%, while the Topix was down 1.12% on Monday. South Korea's Kospi was 1.29% lower, while the small-cap Kosdaq Index fell 0.93%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.37%. The S&P 500 lost nearly 2% last week, its biggest weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, snapping a four-week winning streak. Concerns around the health of the AI trade took center stage after CNBC reported, citing sources, that Anthropic's third-quarter revenue totaled $16.8 billion . And while that's up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, it raised flags among investors about the pace of growth with the AI build-out. Neocloud stock CoreWeave, which uses large amounts of debt to build data centers that it rents out to tech companies, was at the center of those fears. The AI-linked name plummeted 25% last week — its largest one-week drop since November 2025. Investors in the corporate bond market have started to shun CoreWeave, with the company's credit default swaps reaching distress levels . It's not just CoreWeave whose moves in the credit market are concerning. Goldman Sachs traders noted Friday: "AI Credit Spreads and hyperscalers specifically are at the widest levels of the year. The last time spreads were nearly this high, the underlying equities were 15% lower." "The widening across the complex has forced investors to confront what happens as AI spending growth slows. AI Capex has likely peaked and financing, sustainability, and returns on capital have become the debate rather than the next near term earnings revision," they said. "Pessimism is increasing, market breadth is low, and [Friday] we saw the second highest amount of puts traded (right behind June of this year)." Traders were also keeping a wary eye on oil with ship attacks in the Persian Gulf picking up and Ukraine and Russia trading attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine hit an oil terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia on Sunday. Longer-dated oil futures have begun to ratchet higher on expectations energy infrastructure disruptions may last well into 2027. On Sunday however, Brent and WTI crude futures were both trading a tad lower. A slew of earnings from major companies such as Meta Platforms and Tesla hit the Street this week with optimism those results will stabilize the market. 3 Hours Ago Asia-Pacific markets mostly in the red Asia-Pacific markets fell Monday, with Japanese stocks leading declines in the region. Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 1.65%, while the Topix was down 1.12%. South Korea's Kospi was 1.29% lower, while the small-cap Kosdaq Index fell 0.93%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.37%. — Lee Ying Shan 3 Hours Ago EQT's $6.5 billion takeover for Australia's Cleanaway sends its shares surging 20% Shares of Australia's Cleanaway Waste Management surged 19.84% on Monday after Swedish private equity firm EQT announced an agreement to acquire the company in a deal valued at about $9.3 billion Australian dollars ($6.5 billion). Under the agreement, EQT will acquire all outstanding shares of Cleanaway for A$3.095 per share in cash, subject to adjustments for any dividends or other distributions. The offer represents a 32.1% premium to Cleanaway's closing share price of A$2.37 on Aug. 12, the last full trading day before the company first disclosed a potential transaction. EQT said it sees opportunities to invest in Cleanaway's infrastructure and improve the performance of its waste management network to meet Australia's evolving waste management needs. Cleanaway's board unanimously recommended that shareholders vote in favor of the deal, citing the significant premium and certainty of cash consideration, subject to no superior proposal emerging and an independent expert concluding that the transaction is in shareholders' best interests. — Jenny Lee 3 Hours Ago Asia-Pacific markets set to fall as Middle East tensions rise Asia-Pacific markets were set for a subdued Monday as investors weighed renewed threats from Iran . Japan's Nikkei 225 was also set to fall at open, with its Chicago and Osaka futures contracts last at 63,985 and 63,630 respectively, compared with the index's previous close of 65,324.29. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.29% in early trade. Hong Kong market is closed for a holiday. A senior Iranian security official said Sunday that Tehran had drawn up a new military response strategy in the event of further U.S.-Israeli strikes, amid reports of multiple attacks on commercial ships in waters surrounding the Arabian Peninsula. “Iran’s armed forces have prepared a response to any new act of adventurism that would be far more devastating than the 12-day and 40-day wars,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said in a post on X. — Lee Ying Shan Correction: This post has been revised to reflect that Hong Kong market is closed for a holiday.

U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations. In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed. "President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press." "President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added. Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX , is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield . "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal. Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said. Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA . Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high. Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress. "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X . "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."
